questions.question: A loudspeaker makes sound by pushing a cone out and back against the air, again and again. A boy plays one steady note through it and turns up the volume, so the note grows louder. How does the cone's motion change?
questions.answer: It swings farther, just as often
choices: It swings farther, just as often
It swings more often, just as far
It swings farther and more often
It swings farther but less often
questions.context: How far the cone swings sets the sound wave's amplitude, and a bigger amplitude carries more energy and is heard as a louder sound. How many times a second it swings sets the frequency, heard as pitch, so a steady note keeps its frequency however loudly it is played.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (NGSS MS-PS4-1, TEKS 8.8A; map line G8.P7) teaches that a wave's amplitude is tied to the energy it carries, heard in sound as loudness, while frequency is heard as pitch.

questions.question: Marin Mersenne, a French friar, set out the laws of vibrating strings in 1636. He found that of two strings alike in every way but length, the shorter one sounds the higher note. How does the shorter string's vibration differ?
questions.answer: It vibrates more times each second
choices: It vibrates more times each second
It vibrates fewer times each second
It swings farther out to each side
It sends its sound out faster
questions.context: Pitch is set by frequency, the number of vibrations each second, measured in hertz: a string half as long vibrates twice as often and sounds a note an octave higher. Mersenne's book gave the first measured frequency of a note people can hear, about 84 hertz. A string that swings farther sounds louder, not higher, and high and low notes travel at the same speed.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (map line G8.P7) teaches frequency as waves or vibrations per second, measured in hertz and heard as pitch.

questions.question: A student ties one end of a long rope to a post and moves the other end up and down, sending waves along it. Then she moves her hand just as far as before but twice as often each second, and the waves run along the rope at the same speed as before. What happens to the crests?
questions.answer: They lie half as far apart
choices: They lie half as far apart
They lie twice as far apart
They lie just as far apart
They rise twice as high
questions.context: A wave's speed is its frequency times its wavelength, the distance from one crest to the next, so twice as many waves a second, moving no faster, must each be half as long. Sound keeps the same rule: the lowest note people can hear, about 20 hertz, has waves about 17 metres long in air, and the highest, about 20,000 hertz, waves about 17 millimetres long. Her hand moves no farther, so the crests rise no higher.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (NGSS MS-PS4-1; map line G8.P7) teaches wavelength as crest to crest and the simple model relating it to frequency: at the same speed, a higher frequency means a shorter wavelength.

questions.question: Pierre Gassendi timed cannon fired at a distance in 1635, from each flash to its bang, and asked whether a high sound travels faster than a low one. The Paris Academy of Sciences timed cannon along a line 28 kilometres long in 1738 and reported on loud and faint bangs. What did Gassendi and the Academy find?
questions.answer: Neither pitch nor loudness changes the speed
choices: Neither pitch nor loudness changes the speed
Higher and louder sounds both travel faster
Pitch changes the speed, but loudness does not
Loudness changes the speed, but pitch does not
questions.context: Gassendi showed that low and high sounds travel at the same speed, against Aristotle, who had taught that high sounds are faster, and the Academy's team found that a sound's force changes nothing about its speed, which they put at 337 metres a second. Gassendi's own figure, about 478 metres a second, and Marin Mersenne's, about 448, were too high; today's figure for air at 20 degrees Celsius is about 343.
questions.grade_note: 8th-grade sound lessons (map line G8.P7) teach that sound's speed is set by what it travels through, not by its pitch or loudness; the flash-and-bang timings are how it was first measured.

questions.question: Lightning and its thunder begin at the same instant. A hiker sees a flash strike a ridge across a valley and counts nine seconds before the thunder reaches her. About how far away did the lightning strike?
choices: About 3 kilometres
About 9 kilometres
About 27 kilometres
About 300 metres
questions.context: The flash reaches her almost at once, so the nine seconds are the sound's journey. Sound travels about 343 metres a second in air, roughly a kilometre every three seconds, so nine seconds puts the strike about 3 kilometres away. Thunder can usually be heard out to about 16 kilometres.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (map line G8.P7) contrasts sound's speed in air with light's; counting from flash to thunder is the standard classroom use of it.

questions.question: Jean-Daniel Colladon and Charles Sturm hung a bell in the water of Lake Geneva below a boat in the 1820s, and each time it was struck, a flash of gunpowder went off on the boat at the same instant. From a second boat more than 10 kilometres away, they timed the gap between each flash and the bell's sound arriving through the water. How did sound's speed in water compare with its speed in air?
choices: About four times as fast
About forty times as fast
About the same speed
About a quarter as fast
questions.context: They found 1,435 metres a second in the lake's cold, fresh water, more than four times the 343 metres a second of sound in air. Water is far denser than air, and density alone would slow sound down, but water is also far harder to squeeze, and that stiffness wins. Light, by contrast, does slow down in water.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (map line G8.P7, CK2023 G8 Sound Waves) teaches that sound needs a medium and travels at different speeds in gases, liquids and solids.

questions.question: A girl presses her ear to one end of a long steel railing while a boy taps the far end with a stone. She hears the tap twice: first through the steel, then a moment later through the air. Sound runs through steel well over ten times as fast as through air. What makes it so fast in steel?
questions.answer: Its particles are tightly bound to one another
choices: Its particles are tightly bound to one another
Its particles travel along with the sound
Its particles dart about faster than air's
Its particles are lighter than air's
questions.context: A solid's particles are packed close and held in place by strong forces, so steel is very hard to squeeze, and a push on one particle reaches its neighbours almost at once. Iron's particles are in fact heavier than air's, and heavier particles alone would slow sound, but the stiffness wins. As the sound passes, each particle only shakes about its own fixed place.
questions.grade_note: 8th-grade sound lessons (map line G8.P7) explain that sound travels fastest in solids because their particles are close together and strongly linked.

questions.question: Galileo Galilei described a test of light's speed in 1638. Two men with covered lanterns stand on hills far apart. The first uncovers his lantern, the second uncovers his the moment he sees that light, and the first notes how long the answering light takes to reach him. Galileo could not tell whether light takes any time at all. About how far does light travel in one second?
choices: About 3 million kilometres
About 300,000 kilometres
About 30,000 kilometres
About 3,000 kilometres
questions.context: Light travels about 300,000 kilometres a second, so it would cross to a hill a few kilometres off and back in a few hundred-thousandths of a second, far too short a time for anyone to catch by uncovering a lantern. Galileo judged that light, if not instantaneous, is extraordinarily rapid; its speed was first estimated in 1676, from the eclipses of one of Jupiter's moons.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (map line G8.P7) teaches that light and the other electromagnetic waves travel at the speed of light, about 300,000 kilometres a second in empty space.

questions.question: Ole Rømer, a Danish astronomer at the Paris Observatory, timed the moments when Io, a moon of Jupiter, slid out of Jupiter's shadow. In the months when Earth was moving away from Jupiter, Io came out later and later than the tables said, and while Earth was moving toward Jupiter, earlier. What did Rømer conclude in 1676?
questions.answer: Light takes time to cross the space to Earth
choices: Light takes time to cross the space to Earth
Light slows down as it travels farther out
Io slows down while Earth moves away
Jupiter's shadow stretches while Earth moves away
questions.context: When Earth is farther from Jupiter, Io's light has farther to go, so each eclipse is seen later, and Rømer worked out that light needs about 22 minutes to cross the width of Earth's orbit. Light keeps its speed across empty space, and neither Io nor Jupiter's shadow takes any notice of where Earth is. Christiaan Huygens turned the timing into about 220,000 kilometres a second (today's figure is about 300,000), though Giovanni Cassini, Rømer's chief at the observatory, blamed irregular orbits of the moons instead.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (map line G8.P7) teaches light's speed; Rømer's timing of Io is the classic first evidence that light takes time to travel.

questions.question: Ernst Chladni sprinkled sand on a metal plate and drew a violin bow along its edge until the plate rang with a note. The sand bounced off the parts that shook and gathered along lines where the plate stayed still. When he bowed it to sound a much higher note, how did the pattern change?
questions.answer: It broke into more lines, set closer together
choices: It broke into more lines, set closer together
It kept the same lines, only sharper
It drew into fewer lines, set farther apart
It spread out evenly over the whole plate
questions.context: A higher note means more vibrations each second and shorter waves across the plate, so more still lines fit on it: a higher tone gives a more detailed pattern, with more lines and smaller open spaces between them. Chladni published his figures in 1787 and showed them to the Paris Academy in 1808, with Napoleon in the audience.
questions.grade_note: 8th-grade sound lessons (map line G8.P7) link a vibration's frequency to its pitch; Chladni's plates are the classic way to make a sounding object's vibration visible.
